name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q01 - Hydration enthalpy and lithium salt hydration

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Lithium salts such as lithium chloride are commonly hydrated (for example, \(\mathrm{LiCl}\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)), whereas salts of other alkali metals are usually anhydrous.

Reason (R): The \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion has the smallest size among the alkali metal ions and therefore possesses the highest hydration enthalpy.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydration enthalpy of alkali metal ions is inversely related to ionic radius. As ionic size increases down Group 1, the charge density decreases and the attraction for polar water molecules weakens, so hydration enthalpy decreases in the order \(\mathrm{Li}^+ > \mathrm{Na}^+ > \mathrm{K}^+ > \mathrm{Rb}^+ > \mathrm{Cs}^+\).

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Because \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) has the maximum degree of hydration among alkali metal ions, lithium salts readily retain water of crystallisation and commonly exist as hydrates such as \(\mathrm{LiCl}\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), unlike salts of heavier alkali metals such as \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) or \(\mathrm{KCl}\). Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
The \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion has the smallest ionic radius (\(76\text{ pm}\)) in Group 1 and consequently the highest hydration enthalpy (\(-506\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
The high hydration enthalpy arising from the small size of \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) directly causes lithium salts to crystallise as hydrates. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q02 - Density comparison of potassium and sodium

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Potassium is lighter (has a lower density) than sodium.

Reason (R): The atomic mass of potassium is less than that of sodium.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Density is the ratio of mass to volume. Down Group 1, both atomic mass and atomic size (volume) increase, and the relative rates at which they increase determine the density trend.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Although density generally increases down the alkali metal group from \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}\), potassium (\(0.86\text{ g cm}^{-3}\)) is an exception and has a lower density than sodium (\(0.97\text{ g cm}^{-3}\)) because the increase in atomic volume from \(\mathrm{Na}\) to \(\mathrm{K}\) outweighs the increase in atomic mass. Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Potassium has atomic number \(19\) and atomic mass \(39.10\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), which is greater than the atomic mass of sodium (\(22.99\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)). Hence, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is correct, whereas the Reason is incorrect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q03 - Reactivity of lithium and sodium with water

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Although lithium has the most negative standard electrode potential (\(E^\circ\)) among the alkali metals, its reaction with water is less vigorous than that of sodium.

Reason (R): Lithium has a very small size and very high hydration energy.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Standard electrode potential \(E^\circ\) for \(\mathrm{M}^+/\mathrm{M}\) measures the overall thermodynamic tendency of the metal to be oxidised in aqueous solution (involving sublimation, ionisation, and hydration enthalpies), whereas the vigour of reaction with water depends on kinetic and surface factors as well.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Lithium has the most negative \(E^\circ\) value (\(-3.04\text{ V}\)) and sodium has the least negative \(E^\circ\) value (\(-2.714\text{ V}\)) among the alkali metals; nevertheless, lithium reacts with water less vigorously than sodium. Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Lithium possesses a very small atomic and ionic size and consequently a very high hydration energy (\(-506\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
This anomalous behaviour of lithium in reacting less vigorously with water despite its most negative \(E^\circ\) value is attributed to its small size and very high hydration energy. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q04 - Alkali metal solutions in liquid ammonia

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Dilute solutions of alkali metals in liquid ammonia are deep blue in colour and paramagnetic in nature.

Reason (R): On standing, solutions of alkali metals in liquid ammonia slowly liberate dihydrogen gas, resulting in the formation of metal amides.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkali metals dissolve in liquid ammonia according to the equation \(\mathrm{M} + (x + y)\mathrm{NH}_3 \rightarrow [\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_x]^+ + [\mathrm{e}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_y]^-\), forming ammoniated cations and ammoniated electrons.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
The ammoniated electron absorbs energy in the visible region of light, imparting a deep blue colour to the dilute solution, and the presence of unpaired ammoniated electrons makes the solution paramagnetic. Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
On standing, the ammoniated metal ion and electron slowly react with liquid ammonia to form amide and liberate dihydrogen: \(\mathrm{M}^+(\mathrm{am}) + \mathrm{e}^- + \mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{l}) \rightarrow \mathrm{MNH}_2(\mathrm{am}) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\). Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
The deep blue colour and paramagnetism are caused by the ammoniated electrons, not by the slow decomposition to form amides and dihydrogen. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

answer.text: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q05 - Solvay process and potassium carbonate manufacture

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Potassium carbonate (\(\mathrm{K}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)) can be manufactured on a large scale by the Solvay process.

Reason (R): Potassium hydrogencarbonate (\(\mathrm{KHCO}_3\)) is too soluble in water to be precipitated by adding ammonium hydrogencarbonate to a saturated solution of potassium chloride.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Solvay process relies on the low solubility of the intermediate metal hydrogencarbonate so that it precipitates out from an aqueous solution and can be separated and heated to obtain the carbonate.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
While sodium hydrogencarbonate (\(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\)) precipitates in the reaction between \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{HCO}_3\) and \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), the Solvay process cannot be extended to the manufacture of potassium carbonate. Hence, the Assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Potassium hydrogencarbonate (\(\mathrm{KHCO}_3\)) has high solubility in water and does not precipitate when ammonium hydrogencarbonate is added to a saturated \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution. Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is incorrect, whereas the Reason is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q06 - Covalent character of lithium iodide

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Among the lithium halides, lithium iodide (\(\mathrm{LiI}\)) is the most covalent in nature.

Reason (R): The small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion has a high polarising capability, and a large anion such as \(\mathrm{I}^-\) has its electron cloud easily distorted by the cation.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a cation. Greater polarisation leads to greater covalent character in an otherwise ionic compound.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Although alkali metal halides are generally ionic, lithium halides show noticeable covalent character, and among them \(\mathrm{LiI}\) is the most covalent. Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Because \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) is very small, it possesses high polarising power, and among halide ions, \(\mathrm{I}^-\) is the largest and most easily polarised. Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
The ease of distortion of the large \(\mathrm{I}^-\) electron cloud by the small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion directly explains why \(\mathrm{LiI}\) has the highest covalent character among lithium halides. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q07 - Flame test of alkaline earth metals

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Beryllium and magnesium do not impart any characteristic colour to a flame, whereas calcium, strontium, and barium do.

Reason (R): The first ionization enthalpies of alkaline earth metals are higher than those of the corresponding Group 1 alkali metals in the same period.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Flame colouration occurs when thermal energy from the flame excites valence electrons to higher energy levels, and visible light is emitted as they return to the ground state.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Calcium (brick red), strontium (crimson), and barium (apple green) impart characteristic colours to the flame, whereas beryllium and magnesium do not give any flame colour. Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Due to smaller atomic sizes and higher nuclear charge across a period, Group 2 elements have higher first ionisation enthalpies than the corresponding Group 1 elements. Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
Beryllium and magnesium fail to impart flame colour specifically because their valence electrons are too strongly bound to be excited by the energy of the flame, rather than simply because Group 2 first ionisation enthalpies exceed those of Group 1 (which also holds for \(\mathrm{Ca}\), \(\mathrm{Sr}\), and \(\mathrm{Ba}\)). Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q08 - Amphoteric nature and coordination of beryllium

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Beryllium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{Be(OH)}_2\)) is amphoteric in nature and reacts with both acids and alkalies.

Reason (R): Beryllium expands its coordination number to six in its hydroxo complexes by making use of vacant \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An amphoteric hydroxide reacts with both acids and bases. The maximum coordination number of an element is limited by the number of available valence orbitals.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Unlike the hydroxides of other Group 2 elements, \(\mathrm{Be(OH)}_2\) is amphoteric: it reacts with alkali to form the beryllate ion \([\mathrm{Be(OH)}_4]^{2-}\) and with \(\mathrm{HCl}\) in water to form \([\mathrm{Be(OH)}_4]\mathrm{Cl}_2\). Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Beryllium has only four orbitals (\(2s\) and three \(2p\)) in its valence shell and has no \(d\)-orbitals in the second shell; therefore, it cannot exhibit a coordination number greater than four. Hence, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is correct, whereas the Reason is incorrect.

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q09 - Solubility trends of alkaline earth hydroxides and sulphates

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): In Group 2, the solubility of hydroxides in water increases down the group from \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) to \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2\), whereas the solubility of sulphates decreases down the group from \(\mathrm{BeSO}_4\) to \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\).

Reason (R): For hydroxides, lattice enthalpy decreases much more than hydration enthalpy with increasing cationic size, whereas for sulphates, the much larger anion size keeps lattice enthalpy nearly constant down the group while hydration enthalpy decreases.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The aqueous solubility of an ionic salt depends on the balance between lattice enthalpy (energy required to separate ions) and hydration enthalpy (energy released when ions are hydrated). Solubility increases when hydration enthalpy becomes more favourable relative to lattice enthalpy.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Among alkaline earth metal compounds, hydroxides become progressively more soluble down the group, whereas sulphates become less soluble from \(\mathrm{BeSO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{MgSO}_4\) (readily soluble) down to \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\) (insoluble). Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
With the relatively small \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ion, increasing the cationic radius down the group causes a sharper drop in lattice enthalpy than in hydration enthalpy. In contrast, with the much larger \(\mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}\) ion, the inter-ionic distance is dominated by the anion size, so lattice enthalpy stays almost constant down the group while hydration enthalpy decreases as cationic size increases. Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Relationship and Final Conclusion
The opposing relative rates of change in lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpy with anion size directly explain the opposite solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulphates. Therefore, both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q10 - Thermal dehydration of gypsum and Plaster of Paris

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Heating gypsum (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) above \(393\text{ K}\) produces Plaster of Paris, which sets into a hard solid on mixing with water.

Reason (R): Above \(393\text{ K}\), no water of crystallisation is left in gypsum and anhydrous calcium sulphate (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\)), known as dead burnt plaster, is formed.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Controlled heating of gypsum (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) removes water of crystallisation in stages, forming different hydration states of calcium sulphate with distinct setting properties.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Plaster of Paris (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is obtained by heating gypsum to \(393\text{ K}\) according to \(2(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}) \rightarrow 2(\mathrm{CaSO}_4)\cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 3\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\). Heating gypsum above \(393\text{ K}\) does not give Plaster of Paris. Hence, the Assertion is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Above \(393\text{ K}\), all water of crystallisation is lost, yielding anhydrous calcium sulphate (\(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\)), which is called dead burnt plaster. Hence, the Reason is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is incorrect, whereas the Reason is correct.

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_AR_Q11 - Thermal decomposition of lithium and sodium nitrates

questiontext.text:
Assertion (A): Both lithium nitrate and magnesium nitrate decompose on heating to give their respective metal oxides, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen.

Reason (R): Other alkali metal nitrates such as sodium nitrate also decompose on heating to give the corresponding metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Due to the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium (similar ionic sizes and charge/radius ratio), their oxo-salts show parallel thermal decomposition behaviour that differs from heavier alkali metals.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Assertion
Lithium nitrate decomposes on heating as \(4\mathrm{LiNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O} + 4\mathrm{NO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\), and alkaline earth metal nitrates including magnesium nitrate decompose similarly as \(2\mathrm{Mg(NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO} + 4\mathrm{NO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\). Hence, the Assertion is correct.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Reason
Other alkali metal nitrates such as sodium nitrate do not decompose to the oxide; instead, they decompose to form the corresponding metal nitrite and oxygen: \(2\mathrm{NaNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaNO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\). Hence, the Reason is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The Assertion is correct, whereas the Reason is incorrect.

Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
